Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and $U\subseteq M$ open. A **piecewise-smooth path** in $U$ is a continuous map $\gamma:[0,1]\to U$ for which some finite partition $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_n=1$ makes every restriction $\gamma|_{[t_{j-1},t_j]}$ smooth as a map of manifolds with boundary. Its source and target are $\gamma(0)$ and $\gamma(1)$. The collection of all such paths is a set: it is a subset, defined by separation, of the function set from $[0,1]$ to $U$.

Two paths $\gamma_0,\gamma_1$ with the same source $x$ and target $y$ are **thin-homotopic**, written $\gamma_0\sim_{\mathrm{thin}}\gamma_1$, if there is a continuous map $H:[0,1]^2\to U$ and a finite subdivision of the square into compact curvilinear triangles such that $H$ is smooth up to each triangle's boundary, $H(0,t)=\gamma_0(t)$, $H(1,t)=\gamma_1(t)$, $H(s,0)=x$, $H(s,1)=y$, and $\operatorname{rank}(dH_{(s,t)})\le 1$ on every smooth triangle. A **curvilinear triangle** here is a compact region equipped with a smooth parametrization from the standard closed two-simplex, smooth up to its three edges. The rank is the dimension of the image of the differential from the two-dimensional tangent space of the triangle to $T_{H(s,t)}M$. The quotient by this relation is used only after its equivalence and compatibility properties are proved.

A **binary relation** on a set $A$ is a subset $R \subseteq A \times A$
([[def-relation-domain-range-and-field]], [[def-cartesian-product]]); we write
$a \sim b$ for $(a,b) \in R$ and read it "$a$ is related to $b$".

A binary relation $\sim$ on $A$ is an **equivalence relation** when it is reflexive
on $A$, symmetric and transitive ([[def-properties-of-a-relation-on-a-set]]), that
is, when it is

- **reflexive**: $a \sim a$ for every $a \in A$;
- **symmetric**: $a \sim b$ implies $b \sim a$, for all $a, b \in A$;
- **transitive**: $a \sim b$ and $b \sim c$ imply $a \sim c$, for all
  $a, b, c \in A$.

Let $\sim$ be an equivalence relation on $A$. For $a \in A$, the **equivalence
class** of $a$ is the subset

$$[a] \;:=\; \{\, b \in A \;:\; a \sim b \,\} \;\subseteq\; A,$$

and any $b$ with $[b] = C$ is called a **representative** of the class $C$. The
**quotient set** is the set of all classes,

$$A/{\sim} \;:=\; \{\, [a] \;:\; a \in A \,\},$$

a subset of the power set of $A$ ([[def-power-set]]). The map
$\pi : A \to A/{\sim}$ ([[def-function]]) with $\pi(a) = [a]$ is the **quotient
map**; it is surjective by construction ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]).

Under the definable-class convention of
[[def-language-of-set-theory]], every class below is a
formula and every function whose domain may be proper-class-sized is a
definable class-function schema. When its domain is a set, it is an ordinary
set-valued function.

A **category** $\mathcal C$ consists of a class
$\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal C)$ of **objects**, a class
$\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal C)$ of **morphisms**, functions
$\operatorname{dom},\operatorname{cod}:\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal C)\to
\operatorname{Ob}(\mathcal C)$, an **identity morphism**
$1_A:A\to A$ for every object $A$, and a **composite**
$g\circ f:A\to C$ whenever $f:A\to B$ and $g:B\to C$.

These data satisfy, whenever the composites are defined,

$$h\circ(g\circ f)=(h\circ g)\circ f,\qquad 1_B\circ f=f=f\circ1_A.$$

We write $\mathcal C(A,B)$, or $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C}(A,B)$, for the
**hom-collection** of morphisms with domain $A$ and codomain $B$. The object
class is allowed to be empty; then the morphism class is empty and all axioms
are vacuous.

**Morphisms carry their domain and codomain.** A category is often presented the
other way round, by saying what the morphisms from $A$ to $B$ are for each pair
of objects. When it is, $\operatorname{Mor}(\mathcal C)$ is the **disjoint
union** of those hom-collections: a morphism is a triple $(A,B,f)$ with $f$ in
the collection assigned to $(A,B)$, and $\operatorname{dom}$ and
$\operatorname{cod}$ are the first two projections, which are then functions in
the required sense. This is not a technicality that can be dropped. In this
library a function is a set of ordered pairs and does not determine a codomain
([[def-function]]), so the empty function is a function $\varnothing\to B$ for
every $B$ at once; reading the morphisms of $\mathbf{Set}$ as bare functions
would give that one set two different codomains and leave $\operatorname{cod}$
undefined. Every concrete category below whose morphisms are described as
structure-preserving maps is to be read with this tagging, and each hom-collection
is then in canonical bijection with the corresponding collection of untagged
maps, so no size or smallness claim is affected.

derivations.claim: The relation is reflexive because $H(s,t)=\gamma(t)$ has rank at most one and fixed endpoints. It is symmetric by replacing $s$ with $1-s$. If $H_0$ joins $\gamma_0$ to $\gamma_1$ and $H_1$ joins $\gamma_1$ to $\gamma_2$, paste $H_0(2s,t)$ on $0\le s\le\tfrac12$ to $H_1(2s-1,t)$ on $\tfrac12\le s\le1$; their common boundary is the same path $\gamma_1$, so the paste is continuous and piecewise smooth on a finite triangulation, fixes both path endpoints, and has rank at most one on each triangle. Thus the relation is transitive.

If $\gamma_0\sim_{\mathrm{thin}}\gamma_1$ and $\delta_0\sim_{\mathrm{thin}}\delta_1$ with matching endpoints, paste their homotopies on the first and second halves of the path parameter. The shared endpoint is fixed throughout each homotopy, so the paste is continuous and piecewise smooth; on each piece its differential has image contained in the image of the corresponding homotopy differential, hence rank at most one. Therefore $\delta_0*\gamma_0\sim_{\mathrm{thin}}\delta_1*\gamma_1$, and composition of classes is well-defined.

Let $\Gamma$ be the path obtained by placing the three given paths, in order, on the three consecutive thirds of $[0,1]$. Each parenthesized concatenation is $\Gamma\circ\phi_j$ for an increasing piecewise-linear homeomorphism $\phi_j:[0,1]\to[0,1]$; on each affine piece, both $\phi_j$ and $\Gamma$ are smooth. The homotopy $H(s,t)=\Gamma((1-s)\phi_0(t)+s\phi_1(t))$ is fixed at its endpoints. Subdivide the square along the finitely many straight break lines of the two piecewise-linear maps and triangulate the resulting polygons. On each triangle, the argument of $\Gamma$ stays in one smooth path piece, so $H$ is smooth there and its two differential columns are scalar multiples of the single vector $\Gamma'$. Its rank is at most one. Thus the two parenthesizations are thin-homotopic. The same construction between the identity parameter and the parameter map for a path with an inserted constant segment proves both identity laws.

Put $\lambda(t)=2t$ for $0\le t\le\tfrac12$ and $\lambda(t)=2(1-t)$ for $\tfrac12\le t\le1$. Then $t\mapsto\gamma(\lambda(t))$ traverses $\gamma$ and then its reverse. The map $H(s,t)=\gamma((1-s)\lambda(t))$ joins this path to the constant path at $\gamma(0)$ with both endpoints fixed. After triangulating along $t=\tfrac12$, it is smooth on each piece and its differential has rank at most one because both derivatives are scalar multiples of $\dot\gamma$. Reversing $\gamma$ gives the corresponding contraction of the reverse-then-forward path at $\gamma(1)$. Hence $[\bar\gamma]$ is a two-sided inverse of $[\gamma]$.

The tagged morphism set has well-defined domain and codomain by construction; step 2.1 makes composition independent of representatives, step 3.1 gives associativity, and step 3.2 gives the inverse axiom. Steps 3.1 and 3.2 also provide the two identity laws stated in [F3]. Thus the data form a category in which every morphism is invertible, which is the asserted groupoid.

citations.quote: A **groupoid** is a category in which every morphism has a two-sided inverse. For an open subset $U$ of a smooth manifold, the **thin path groupoid** $\Pi^{\mathrm{thin}}_1(U)$ is the category whose objects are the points of $U$ and whose morphisms from $x$ to $y$ are tagged triples $(x,y,[\gamma])$, where $[\gamma]$ is a thin-homotopy class of piecewise-smooth paths from $x$ to $y$; composition, identities, and inverses are those of Proposition [[prop-gr-fx-thin-path-quotient-groupoid]].

Let $F:M^m\to N^n$ be smooth, let $q\in N$ be a regular value, and assume
$F^{-1}(q)$ is nonempty. Then $F^{-1}(q)$ is an embedded submanifold of
codimension $n$. Equivalently, it has dimension $m-n$.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and $k\ge 0$. A **smooth differential $k$-form**
on $M$ is a smooth section of $\bigwedge^kT^*M\to M$. The space of such forms
is denoted $\Omega^k(M)$, and $\Omega^0(M)=C^\infty(M)$.

For $\omega\in\Omega^k(M)$, define the candidate $d\omega$ on smooth vector fields by $$d\omega(X_0,\ldots,X_k)=\sum_i(-1)^iX_i\omega(X_0,\widehat X_i,\ldots,X_k)+\sum_{i<j}(-1)^{i+j}\omega([X_i,X_j],X_0,\widehat X_i,\widehat X_j,\ldots,X_k).$$ The next lemma proves that this candidate is a form.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold, possibly with boundary. For $k\ge1$, $c\in C_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$ and $\omega\in\Omega^{k-1}(M)$, define integration over a chain by the finite linear sum of its simplex integrals. Then
$$\int_c d\omega=\int_{\partial c}\omega.$$
The zero chain has integral zero. In degree zero the boundary is zero; no degree-minus-one form is required by this statement.

Define the smooth one-form $\alpha=x\,dy-y\,dx$ using [F3]. For the ambient coordinate vector fields, [F4] gives $d\alpha(\partial_x,\partial_y)=\partial_x(\alpha(\partial_y))-\partial_y(\alpha(\partial_x))-\alpha([\partial_x,\partial_y])=1-(-1)-0=2$, hence $d\alpha=2\,dx\wedge dy$. Every alternating two-form on a one-dimensional tangent space vanishes, so the restriction has $d\alpha=0$ on $S^1$. Along $\gamma$, $x=\cos(2\pi t)$ and $y=\sin(2\pi t)$ give $\alpha(\dot\gamma(t))=2\pi$ and $\int_\gamma\alpha=2\pi$; the constant loop has integral zero.

Suppose a thin homotopy $H:[0,1]^2\to S^1$ joined $\gamma$ to the constant loop while fixing the basepoint at the path endpoints. Apply [F5] to each smooth curvilinear triangle of a finite subdivision and sum; internal oriented edges cancel. Since [F4] and step 1.1 give $d\alpha=0$, Stokes gives $\int_{\partial[0,1]^2}H^*\alpha=0$. The two path edges have signed integral $2\pi$ or $-2\pi$ because one is $\gamma$ and the other is constant; the endpoint edges are constant and contribute zero. The nonzero boundary integral contradicts Stokes. Thus $[\gamma]$ is not the identity class.

Let $M$ be a smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold, $U\subseteq M$ a nonempty open set with a smooth tetrad, and $\omega$ its Lorentz-connection matrix from [[def-gr-fx-tetrad-spin-connection]]. Assume the supplier's $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention. For a piecewise-smooth path $\gamma:[0,1]\to U$, let $A_\gamma(t)=\omega_{\gamma(t)}(\dot\gamma(t))$ on each smooth piece. By Proposition [[prop-gr-fx-connection-path-transport-exists]], there is a unique continuous piecewise-$C^1$ solution

$$\dot U_\gamma(t)=-A_\gamma(t)U_\gamma(t),\qquad U_\gamma(0)=I_4.$$

The endpoint matrix $U_\gamma(1)$ is the **connection path transport** in the chosen tetrad trivialization. It maps vector components at $\gamma(0)$ to components at $\gamma(1)$ under the convention of the supplier. A smooth local Lorentz frame change transforms this matrix by its endpoint frame matrices; it is a gauge transformation in the principal-bundle sense only if it extends to an automorphism over the identity as in [[def-gauge-group-of-a-smooth-principal-bundle]].

[[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]]. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth,

$U\subseteq M$ be nonempty and open, and let

$E_J$ are a pointwise basis of $TM|_U$, $g(E_I,E_J)=\eta_{IJ}$ for
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and $E_0$ is future-directed. Write
$e=(e^0,e^1,e^2,e^3)^{\mathsf T}$ for the dual coframe, so
$e^I(E_J)=\delta^I{}_J$.

A **tetrad connection** is a smooth affine connection $\nabla$ on $TM|_U$;
its connection matrix $\omega=(\omega^I{}_J)$ in $E$ is defined by
$\nabla_XE_J=\sum_I\omega^I{}_J(X)E_I$. It is a **Lorentz connection** when
it is metric-compatible, equivalently when the matrix-valued one-form is
$\eta$-skew: $\omega_{IJ}:=\eta_{IK}\omega^K{}_J$ satisfies
$\omega_{IJ}=-\omega_{JI}$. A smooth local Lorentz change is a smooth map
$\Lambda:U\to SO^+(1,3)$. With the convention
$e'=\Lambda e$ (equivalently $E'=E\Lambda^{-1}$), the connection matrix
transforms as

$$e'=\Lambda e,\qquad \omega'=\Lambda\omega\Lambda^{-1}-d\Lambda\,\Lambda^{-1}.$$

Here $d$ is the componentwise exterior derivative, and products of
matrix-valued forms use matrix multiplication and the wedge product of their
scalar form entries. Define the torsion and curvature forms by

$$T^I:=de^I+\sum_J\omega^I{}_J\wedge e^J,\qquad F^I{}_J:=d\omega^I{}_J+\sum_K\omega^I{}_K\wedge\omega^K{}_J.$$

Thus $T$ is an $\mathbb R^4$-valued two-form and $F$ is an
$\operatorname{End}(\mathbb R^4)$-valued two-form. With this convention,

change of frame in a trivialization; it represents a gauge transformation in
the sense of [[def-gauge-group-of-a-smooth-principal-bundle]] only when it
extends to a principal-bundle automorphism over the identity. No such extension,
global tetrad, or spin structure is part of this definition.

Let $X$ be a topological space and let $x_0\in X$. A **based loop at $x_0$**
is a path $\alpha:I\to X$ with $\alpha(0)=x_0=\alpha(1)$
([[def-path-connected]]). Two based loops are equivalent when they are
path-homotopic relative to the endpoints. This is an equivalence relation by
[[cor-homotopy-relative-and-path-homotopy-are-equivalence-relations]].

The **fundamental group set** of $X$ at $x_0$ is

$$\pi_1(X,x_0):=\{\,[\alpha]:\alpha\text{ is a based loop at }x_0\,\}.$$

For composable paths, write

$$(\alpha*\beta)(s):=\begin{cases}\alpha(2s),&0\leq s\leq\tfrac12,\\ \beta(2s-1),&\tfrac12\leq s\leq1.\end{cases}$$

The finite closed-pasting argument already carried out in
[[def-path-connected]] shows that this is a path. The multiplication proposed
on loop classes is

$$[\alpha][\beta]:=[\alpha*\beta].$$

**Order convention.** The product $[\alpha][\beta]$ traverses $\alpha$ first
and $\beta$ second. Every product on this page uses this convention.

The constant loop at $x_0$ is denoted $c_{x_0}$, and the reversed loop is
$\bar\alpha(s):=\alpha(1-s)$. The next theorem proves that multiplication is

By Proposition [[prop-gr-fx-connection-path-transport-exists]], there is a unique continuous piecewise-$C^1$ solution

$$\dot U_\gamma(t)=-A_\gamma(t)U_\gamma(t),\qquad U_\gamma(0)=I_4.$$

The endpoint matrix $U_\gamma(1)$ is the **connection path transport** in the chosen tetrad trivialization. It maps vector components at $\gamma(0)$ to components at $\gamma(1)$ under the convention of the supplier. A smooth local Lorentz frame change transforms this matrix by its endpoint frame matrices; it is a gauge transformation in the principal-bundle sense only if it extends to an automorphism over the identity as in [[def-gauge-group-of-a-smooth-principal-bundle]].

A **groupoid** is a category in which every morphism has a two-sided inverse. For an open subset $U$ of a smooth manifold, the **thin path groupoid** $\Pi^{\mathrm{thin}}_1(U)$ is the category whose objects are the points of $U$ and whose morphisms from $x$ to $y$ are tagged triples $(x,y,[\gamma])$, where $[\gamma]$ is a thin-homotopy class of piecewise-smooth paths from $x$ to $y$; composition, identities, and inverses are those of Proposition [[prop-gr-fx-thin-path-quotient-groupoid]].

Under the assumptions of [[def-gr-fx-connection-path-transport]], if two piecewise-smooth paths $\gamma_0,\gamma_1:[0,1]\to U$ are thin-homotopic in the sense of [[def-gr-fx-thin-paths]], then $U_{\gamma_0}(1)=U_{\gamma_1}(1)$ in the fixed tetrad trivialization.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the canonical tangent-bundle and tetrad
conventions of [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] and
[[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]]. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth,
time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$, let
$U\subseteq M$ be nonempty and open, and let
$E=(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$ be a smooth future-directed tetrad on $U$. Thus the
$E_J$ are a pointwise basis of $TM|_U$, $g(E_I,E_J)=\eta_{IJ}$ for
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and $E_0$ is future-directed. Write
$e=(e^0,e^1,e^2,e^3)^{\mathsf T}$ for the dual coframe, so
$e^I(E_J)=\delta^I{}_J$.

A **tetrad connection** is a smooth affine connection $\nabla$ on $TM|_U$;
its connection matrix $\omega=(\omega^I{}_J)$ in $E$ is defined by
$\nabla_XE_J=\sum_I\omega^I{}_J(X)E_I$. It is a **Lorentz connection** when
it is metric-compatible, equivalently when the matrix-valued one-form is
$\eta$-skew: $\omega_{IJ}:=\eta_{IK}\omega^K{}_J$ satisfies
$\omega_{IJ}=-\omega_{JI}$. A smooth local Lorentz change is a smooth map
$\Lambda:U\to SO^+(1,3)$. With the convention
$e'=\Lambda e$ (equivalently $E'=E\Lambda^{-1}$), the connection matrix

$$e'=\Lambda e,\qquad \omega'=\Lambda\omega\Lambda^{-1}-d\Lambda\,\Lambda^{-1}.$$

matrix-valued forms use matrix multiplication and the wedge product of their
scalar form entries. Define the torsion and curvature forms by

$$T^I:=de^I+\sum_J\omega^I{}_J\wedge e^J,\qquad F^I{}_J:=d\omega^I{}_J+\sum_K\omega^I{}_K\wedge\omega^K{}_J.$$

the sense of [[def-gauge-group-of-a-smooth-principal-bundle]] only when it
extends to a principal-bundle automorphism over the identity. No such extension,
global tetrad, or spin structure is part of this definition.

($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

A **finite oriented graph** consists of finite vertex and edge sets $V,E$, source and target maps $s,t:E\to V$, and a fixed-point-free involution $e\mapsto\bar e$ with $s(\bar e)=t(e)$ and $t(\bar e)=s(e)$. A **finite SU(2) graph configuration** assigns $g_e\in SU(2)$ to every oriented edge and requires $g_{\bar e}=g_e^{-1}$. A graph path is a finite composable edge word $e_1,\ldots,e_n$; its holonomy is the later-left product $g_{e_n}\cdots g_{e_1}$, and the empty path has holonomy $I_2$.

A vertex gauge assignment is a function $h:V\to SU(2)$. It acts on edge variables by

$$g_e\longmapsto g'_e=h_{t(e)}g_eh_{s(e)}^{-1}.$$

A **finite-dimensional unitary representation** is a continuous group homomorphism $\rho:SU(2)\to U(W)$ for a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space $W$, where

$$U(W):=\{T\in\operatorname{GL}(W):\langle Tv,Tw\rangle=\langle v,w\rangle\text{ for all }v,w\in W\}.$$

derivations.claim: The vertex action preserves the reverse-edge condition because $g'_{\bar e}=h_{s(e)}g_e^{-1}h_{t(e)}^{-1}=(h_{t(e)}g_eh_{s(e)}^{-1})^{-1}=(g'_e)^{-1}$. Thus the transformed variables are again a graph configuration.

If the path is empty, its product is $I_2$ before and after the gauge action, so its trace is unchanged. For the rest of the proof assume the closed path has $n\ge1$ edges and write it as $e_1:v_0\to v_1,\ldots,e_n:v_{n-1}\to v_n=v_0$.

The transformed product is $g'_{e_n}\cdots g'_{e_1}=h_{v_0}g_{e_n}h_{v_{n-1}}^{-1}h_{v_{n-1}}g_{e_{n-1}}\cdots h_{v_1}^{-1}h_{v_1}g_{e_1}h_{v_0}^{-1}=h_{v_0}(g_{e_n}\cdots g_{e_1})h_{v_0}^{-1}$; all adjacent intermediate factors cancel because $h_v^{-1}h_v=I$.

Applying the homomorphism $\rho$ carries this conjugation to conjugation by $\rho(h_{v_0})$. For finite matrices, $\operatorname{Tr}(AB)=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}B_{ji}=\operatorname{Tr}(BA)$; take $A=\rho(h_{v_0})$ and $B=\rho(g_{e_n}\cdots g_{e_1})\rho(h_{v_0})^{-1}$ to obtain the same trace as before. Let $M_2(\mathbb C)$ have its Euclidean topology as $\mathbb R^8$, and define

$$SU(2)=\{Q\in M_2(\mathbb C):Q^\dagger Q=I_2,\ \det Q=1\}.$$

Under matrix multiplication, $SU(2)$ is a compact Hausdorff topological group.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $\rho:G\to\operatorname{GL}(V)$ and $\sigma:G\to\operatorname{GL}(W)$ be
finite-dimensional complex representations of a group $G$
([[def-finite-dimensional-representation-of-a-group-over-a-field]]). Their
**tensor product representation** $\rho\otimes\sigma$ is the representation of
$G$ on the complex tensor product $V\otimes_{\mathbb C}W$ given on elementary
tensors by

$$g\cdot(v\otimes w):=\bigl(\rho(g)v\bigr)\otimes\bigl(\sigma(g)w\bigr)\qquad(g\in G,\ v\in V,\ w\in W).$$

**The action is well defined.** For fixed $g\in G$, the assignment
$(v,w)\mapsto\rho(g)v\otimes\sigma(g)w$ is additive in each variable and
$\mathbb C$-balanced, because $\rho(g)$ and $\sigma(g)$ are $\mathbb C$-linear:
$\rho(g)(v\lambda)\otimes\sigma(g)w=(\rho(g)v)\lambda\otimes\sigma(g)w$. By
[[thm-universal-property-of-module-tensor-products]] there is a unique
$\mathbb C$-linear map $\rho(g)\otimes\sigma(g):V\otimes_{\mathbb C}W\to
V\otimes_{\mathbb C}W$ with the displayed value on every elementary tensor.
Because the two sides of
$g\cdot(h\cdot(v\otimes w))=(gh)\cdot(v\otimes w)$ agree on every elementary
tensor and the elementary tensors span $V\otimes_{\mathbb C}W$, the assignment
$g\mapsto\rho(g)\otimes\sigma(g)$ is a group homomorphism into
$\operatorname{GL}(V\otimes_{\mathbb C}W)$, with
$\rho(1)\otimes\sigma(1)=\operatorname{id}$. The underlying space is
finite-dimensional: bases of $V$ and $W$ give the basis
$(v_i\otimes w_j)_{i,j}$, so $\dim(V\otimes_{\mathbb C}W)=(\dim V)(\dim W)$.

Let $\rho:G\to\operatorname{GL}(V)$ be a finite-dimensional complex
representation of a group $G$
([[def-finite-dimensional-representation-of-a-group-over-a-field]]). Its
**dual** or **contragredient** representation is the representation $\rho^{*}$
of $G$ on the algebraic dual space $V^{*}$
([[def-algebraic-dual-and-linear-functional]]) defined by

$$\bigl(g\cdot f\bigr)(v):=f\bigl(g^{-1}\cdot v\bigr)\qquad(g\in G,\ f\in V^{*},\ v\in V),$$

equivalently $g\cdot f=f\circ\rho(g^{-1})$.

Each operator $\rho^{*}(g)$ is $\mathbb C$-linear because $f$ and
$\rho(g^{-1})$ are. The inverse appears so that composition is
order-preserving: writing $g\cdot f=f\circ\rho(g^{-1})$,

$$(gh)\cdot f=f\circ\rho\bigl((gh)^{-1}\bigr)=f\circ\rho(h^{-1})\circ\rho(g^{-1})=g\cdot(h\cdot f),$$

and $1\cdot f=f\circ\operatorname{id}_V=f$. Hence $\rho^{*}$ is a group
homomorphism $G\to\operatorname{GL}(V^{*})$, a representation of the same
degree as $\rho$.
Assume AC. Every compact Hausdorff group has a unique left Haar probability measure. It is right invariant and inversion invariant as well.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ whose induced-length metric is complete: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm (Banach space).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
Banach space defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
(Real and imaginary parts, complex conjugation, and modulus). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of Real and complex inner product spaces, with the inner product linear in the first argument: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published The norm $\lVert v\rVert=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ induced by a real or complex inner product: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

Let $G$ be a topological group and $H$ a complex Hilbert space. A
**unitary representation** of $G$ on $H$ is a group homomorphism
$\pi:G\to U(H)$, where $U(H)$ is the group of bijective complex-linear
isometries of $H$, such that the orbit map $g\mapsto\pi(g)v$ is norm-continuous
for every $v\in H$. This condition is **strong continuity**. A closed linear
subspace $M\subseteq H$ is **invariant** if $\pi(g)M=M$ for every $g\in G$.
The representation is **irreducible** if $H\ne\{0\}$ and its only closed
invariant linear subspaces are $\{0\}$ and $H$.

For unitary representations $\pi$ on $H$ and $\rho$ on $K$, a **bounded
intertwiner** is a bounded linear operator $T:H\to K$ satisfying
$$T\pi(g)=\rho(g)T\qquad(g\in G).$$
The representations are **unitarily equivalent** if there is a unitary
intertwiner between them. The **commutant** of $\pi$ is
$$\pi(G)'=\{T\in\mathcal B(H):T\pi(g)=\pi(g)T\text{ for every }g\in G\}.$$

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]. A $\mathbb K$-linear map
$T:X\to Y$ ([[def-linear-map]]) is a **bounded linear operator** when there is a
real constant $C \ge 0$ such that

$$\|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X.$$

Any such $C$ is called a **bound** for $T$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $K$ be a compact
Hausdorff group with normalized Haar probability measure $\mu$
([[cor-normalized-haar-probability-on-a-compact-group]]). Under the assumed
Axiom of Choice the Axiom of Countable Choice holds as well
([[lem-ac-supplies-countable-and-dependent-choice-for-banach-integration]]).

Let $\pi:K\to U(H)$ and $\sigma:K\to U(J)$ be strongly continuous unitary
representations of $K$ on complex Hilbert spaces $H$ and $J$
([[def-strongly-continuous-unitary-representation]], [[def-hilbert-space]]),
and let $T\in\mathcal B(H,J)$ be a bounded linear operator
([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). The pairing below is linear in the first
variable and conjugate-linear in the second
([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]).

**The scalar integrals.** Fix $v\in H$ and $w\in J$ and put

$$b_v(w):=\int_K\langle\sigma(k)T\pi(k)^{-1}v,\,w\rangle\,d\mu(k).$$

The integrand is continuous on $K$. Indeed, $k\mapsto T\pi(k)^{-1}v$ is
continuous because $\pi$ is strongly continuous and $T$ is bounded, and for a
continuous map $\psi$ into $J$ the map $k\mapsto\sigma(k)\psi(k)$ is continuous
because every $\sigma(k)$ is an isometry: for fixed $k_0$,

$$\|\sigma(k)\psi(k)-\sigma(k_0)\psi(k_0)\|\le\|\psi(k)-\psi(k_0)\|+\|(\sigma(k)-\sigma(k_0))\psi(k_0)\|,$$

and both terms tend to zero as $k\to k_0$. A continuous complex function on the
compact space $K$ is bounded and Borel, so the displayed integral is a finite
complex number; and $\bigl|\langle\sigma(k)T\pi(k)^{-1}v,w\rangle\bigr|\le
\|T\|\,\|v\|\,\|w\|$ for every $k$ by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality
([[thm-cauchy-schwarz-in-an-inner-product-space]]), so
$|b_v(w)|\le\|T\|\,\|v\|\,\|w\|$. For fixed $v$ the assignment
$w\mapsto b_v(w)$ is conjugate-linear and $\|w\|\mapsto\|b_v(w)\|$ is bounded
by $\|T\|\,\|v\|$; hence

$$\varphi_v(w):=\overline{b_v(w)}=\int_K\langle w,\sigma(k)T\pi(k)^{-1}v\rangle\,d\mu(k)$$

is a bounded linear functional on $J$ of norm at most $\|T\|\,\|v\|$.

**The definition.** Under Countable Choice the Hilbert space $J$ has the Riesz
representation property ([[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]]): there
is a unique vector $A(T)v\in J$ with $\varphi_v(w)=\langle w,A(T)v\rangle$ for
every $w\in J$, equivalently

$$\langle A(T)v,w\rangle=b_v(w)=\int_K\langle\sigma(k)T\pi(k)^{-1}v,\,w\rangle\,d\mu(k)\qquad(v\in H,\ w\in J).$$

This determines $A(T)$ as a map $H\to J$, the **Haar average** of $T$ with
respect to the pair $(\sigma,\pi)$.

**Well-definedness.** For each $v$ the vector $A(T)v$ is unique, so $A(T)$ is a
well-defined function. It is linear: if $v=a v_1+b v_2$ then, by the
conjugate-linearity in $f$ of the representing vector recorded in
[[thm-riesz-representation-for-hilbert-space]], the vector representing
$\varphi_{av_1+bv_2}=\overline a\,\varphi_{v_1}+\overline b\,\varphi_{v_2}$ is
$aA(T)v_1+bA(T)v_2$; and $\|A(T)v\|=\|\varphi_v\|\le\|T\|\,\|v\|$ because the
Riesz representation is isometric, so $A(T)$ is a bounded linear operator with
$\|A(T)\|\le\|T\|$. The assignment $A$ is itself linear in $T$: for fixed $v,w$
the integrand is linear in $T$, so the scalar integral is, and equality of the
weak matrix elements together with uniqueness of the Riesz vector gives
$A(aT+bT')=aA(T)+bA(T')$. Thus
$A:\mathcal B(H,J)\to\mathcal B(H,J)$ is a well-defined map.

**This is a weak operator integral.** Only scalar functions are integrated in
the definition: for fixed $v$ and $w$, the continuous function
$k\mapsto\langle\sigma(k)T\pi(k)^{-1}v,w\rangle$ is integrated against the
scalar measure $\mu$, and the vector $A(T)v$ is then produced by the Riesz
representation theorem. No operator-norm continuity of the orbit
$k\mapsto\sigma(k)T\pi(k)^{-1}$ of an arbitrary bounded operator $T$ is assumed
or asserted. For finite-rank $T:H\to J$, it follows from
[[lem-conjugation-orbits-of-finite-rank-operators-are-norm-continuous]] as
follows. Equip $H\oplus J$ with the sum inner product; it is a Hilbert space
because Cauchy sequences converge in each coordinate. The representation
$\tau(k)(v,w)=(\pi(k)v,\sigma(k)w)$ is unitary and strongly continuous.
The bounded finite-rank operator $S(v,w)=(0,Tv)$ satisfies
$\tau(k)S\tau(k)^{-1}(v,w)=(0,\sigma(k)T\pi(k)^{-1}v)$.
The cited lemma makes this conjugation orbit norm continuous, and restriction
to $H\oplus\{0\}$ followed by projection onto $J$ does not increase operator
norm, proving the claimed continuity for $T$. Only
the Axiom of Choice is used, through normalized Haar measure and Countable
Choice. That $A$ is an idempotent contraction onto the bounded intertwiners,
with operator norm one exactly when $\operatorname{Hom}_K(H,J)\ne\{0\}$, is the
content of [[lem-haar-averaging-projects-onto-the-intertwiner-space]], which
justifies the present definition.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $K$ be a compact
Hausdorff group with normalized Haar probability measure $\mu$
([[cor-normalized-haar-probability-on-a-compact-group]]), and let
$\pi:K\to U(H)$ and $\sigma:K\to U(J)$ be strongly continuous unitary
representations of $K$ on complex Hilbert spaces $H$ and $J$
([[def-strongly-continuous-unitary-representation]], [[def-hilbert-space]]).
Write
$$\operatorname{Hom}_K(H,J):=\{T\in\mathcal B(H,J):T\pi(g)=\sigma(g)T\text{ for every }g\in K\}$$
for the space of bounded intertwiners and let
$A:\mathcal B(H,J)\to\mathcal B(H,J)$ be the Haar averaging operator of
[[def-haar-averaging-operator-on-hom-spaces]], so that
$$\langle A(T)v,w\rangle=\int_K\langle\sigma(k)T\pi(k)^{-1}v,w\rangle\,d\mu(k)$$
for all $T\in\mathcal B(H,J)$, $v\in H$, $w\in J$. Then:

1. $A$ is idempotent, $A\circ A=A$, and its range is exactly
   $\operatorname{Hom}_K(H,J)$: $A(T)$ intertwines for every bounded $T$, and
   $A(T)=T$ for every bounded intertwiner $T$;
2. $A$ is a contraction, $\|A(T)\|\le\|T\|$ for every $T\in\mathcal B(H,J)$,
   hence $\|A\|\le1$;
3. $\|A\|=1$ if $\operatorname{Hom}_K(H,J)\ne\{0\}$, and $\|A\|=0$ if
   $\operatorname{Hom}_K(H,J)=\{0\}$.

derivations.claim: For each dual factor, choose an orthonormal basis of $V_e$ and use its dual-basis inner product; this is basis-independent because a change between orthonormal bases preserves the Euclidean coefficient norm. The matrix of the dual action is the transpose of the inverse unitary matrix, hence is unitary. Tensor products of orthonormal bases are an orthonormal basis for the displayed tensor inner product, so the diagonal action is unitary by [F3]–[F4]. Its matrix entries are finite sums and products of continuous entries of the edge representations, so [F7] makes $R_v$ strongly continuous.

For fixed $w\in W_v$, define $T_w:\mathbb C\to W_v$ by $T_w(z)=zw$, with the trivial representation on $\mathbb C$. It is linear and bounded by [F8], with $\|T_w\|=\|w\|$. The intertwining equation $T_w(z)=R_v(g)T_w(z)$ for all $z$ is equivalent to $w\in W_v^{SU(2)}$.

By [F1], $SU(2)$ is compact Hausdorff; by [F2] and [F5], its normalized Haar probability exists under the stated full AC assumption. The hypotheses of [F9]–[F10] now hold for $H=\mathbb C$, $J=W_v$, and $T=T_w$, using [F6], [F7], and steps 1.1–1.2. Since the trivial representation acts as the identity, the weak Haar average of $T_w$ is $T_{P_vw}$, where the finite-dimensional vector integral is defined coordinatewise. The range clause of [F10] therefore gives $P_v^2=P_v$, $\|P_v\|\le1$, and $\operatorname{ran}P_v=W_v^{SU(2)}$.

If $x\in\operatorname{ran}P_v$ and $y\in\ker P_v$, then $P_v(x+ty)=x$ for every complex scalar $t$. Contractivity gives $\|x\|\le\|x+ty\|$. Squaring and taking real $t$ of both signs forces $\operatorname{Re}\langle x,y\rangle=0$; taking $t$ purely imaginary of both signs forces $\operatorname{Im}\langle x,y\rangle=0$. Hence range and kernel are orthogonal. Since an idempotent has $W_v=\operatorname{ran}P_v\oplus\ker P_v$, $P_v$ is the orthogonal projection onto its invariant range.

On $W=\bigotimes_vW_v$, each vertex operator acts as $P_v$ on one factor and identity on the others. Operators on distinct tensor factors commute, so their product is an idempotent whose range is $\bigotimes_v\operatorname{ran}P_v$, the tensors invariant under every vertex action. It is the orthogonal projection onto this joint invariant subspace because tensor products of orthogonal projections are orthogonal projections in the product Hilbert structure. If the graph has no vertices, the empty product is the identity on $\mathbb C$, consistent with the statement.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ for the canonical tangent-bundle and tetrad
conventions of [[def-gr-smooth-lorentzian-objects]] and
[[def-gr-local-frame-and-tetrad-fields]]. Let $(M,g,N)$ be a smooth,
time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold of signature $(-,+,+,+)$, let
$U\subseteq M$ be nonempty and open, and let
$E=(E_0,E_1,E_2,E_3)$ be a smooth future-directed tetrad on $U$. Thus the
$E_J$ are a pointwise basis of $TM|_U$, $g(E_I,E_J)=\eta_{IJ}$ for
$\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, and $E_0$ is future-directed. Write
$e=(e^0,e^1,e^2,e^3)^{\mathsf T}$ for the dual coframe, so
$e^I(E_J)=\delta^I{}_J$.

A **tetrad connection** is a smooth affine connection $\nabla$ on $TM|_U$;
its connection matrix $\omega=(\omega^I{}_J)$ in $E$ is defined by
$\nabla_XE_J=\sum_I\omega^I{}_J(X)E_I$. It is a **Lorentz connection** when
it is metric-compatible, equivalently when the matrix-valued one-form is
$\eta$-skew: $\omega_{IJ}:=\eta_{IK}\omega^K{}_J$ satisfies
$\omega_{IJ}=-\omega_{JI}$. A smooth local Lorentz change is a smooth map
$\Lambda:U\to SO^+(1,3)$. With the convention
$e'=\Lambda e$ (equivalently $E'=E\Lambda^{-1}$), the connection matrix
transforms as

$$e'=\Lambda e,\qquad \omega'=\Lambda\omega\Lambda^{-1}-d\Lambda\,\Lambda^{-1}.$$

Here $d$ is the componentwise exterior derivative, and products of
matrix-valued forms use matrix multiplication and the wedge product of their
scalar form entries. Define the torsion and curvature forms by

$$T^I:=de^I+\sum_J\omega^I{}_J\wedge e^J,\qquad F^I{}_J:=d\omega^I{}_J+\sum_K\omega^I{}_K\wedge\omega^K{}_J.$$

Thus $T$ is an $\mathbb R^4$-valued two-form and $F$ is an
$\operatorname{End}(\mathbb R^4)$-valued two-form. With this convention,
$F$ is the local curvature two-form of $\nabla$. A local $\Lambda$ is a
change of frame in a trivialization; it represents a gauge transformation in
the sense of [[def-gauge-group-of-a-smooth-principal-bundle]] only when it
extends to a principal-bundle automorphism over the identity. No such extension,
global tetrad, or spin structure is part of this definition.

Let $M$ be a smooth time-oriented Lorentzian four-manifold, $U\subseteq M$ a nonempty open set with a smooth tetrad, and $\omega$ its Lorentz-connection matrix from [[def-gr-fx-tetrad-spin-connection]]. Assume the supplier's $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ convention. For a piecewise-smooth path $\gamma:[0,1]\to U$, let $A_\gamma(t)=\omega_{\gamma(t)}(\dot\gamma(t))$ on each smooth piece. By Proposition [[prop-gr-fx-connection-path-transport-exists]], there is a unique continuous piecewise-$C^1$ solution

$$\dot U_\gamma(t)=-A_\gamma(t)U_\gamma(t),\qquad U_\gamma(0)=I_4.$$
